h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: Large batches divide the L2 gradient by a big batch size and take few steps, so raising alpha barely changes effective regularization and costs little accuracy.
When LR is too small to fit within 243 epochs, extra width speeds loss reduction and partially compensates for undertraining.
Large batches leave few optimization steps, and wider nets reduce loss faster per step, so width substitutes for missing steps.
A single-hidden-layer net gets capacity only from width, so widening matters more there than in deeper nets that already draw capacity from depth.
Strong L2 already caps usable capacity, so removing units costs little when the penalty rather than the architecture is the bottleneck.
With batches of 161-256 there are too few update steps for a deeper, slower-to-optimize net to converge in 243 epochs.
Deeper ReLU stacks have compounding Jacobians and sharper curvature, so high LR causes divergence or dead units more often in them.
Heavy L2 applied to every layer compounds multiplicatively through depth, so adding a layer under strong shrinkage collapses signal propagation.
At tiny LR the net is already undertrained, so cutting the number of update steps with a larger batch hurts fitting more.
Large batches give low-noise gradients but few steps, so a bigger LR both is tolerated and compensates for the reduced step count.
